title: What heat illness training does Cal/OSHA require for outdoor and indoor workers?
description: Title 8 sections 3395(h) and 3396(h): heat training before exposure, nine required topics, supervisor training and indoor thresholds, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: California's outdoor heat standard, title 8 section 3395(h), and its indoor heat standard, section 3396(h), require effective heat illness training for every supervisory and non-supervisory employee before they begin work reasonably expected to expose them to heat illness risk. Training covers nine topics, from risk factors and water intake to emergency procedures. Supervisors need additional training before they supervise that work. The indoor standard has been operative since July 23, 2024.
keyTakeaways: Section 3395 applies to all outdoor places of employment; section 3396 applies to indoor work areas at or above 82 degrees Fahrenheit when employees are present.
Training must happen before the employee begins work with heat illness risk, not at the start of summer or once a year.
Both standards list the same nine employee topics, including drinking small quantities of water up to four cups per hour and the right to use the standard without retaliation.

Supervisors must be trained before supervising heat-exposed work, including how to respond to symptoms; outdoor supervisors must know how to monitor weather reports and respond to hot weather advisories.
The written Heat Illness Prevention Plan must be in English and in the language understood by the majority of employees, and may be part of the IIPP.
regulator: California Division of Occupational Safety and Health (Cal/OSHA), Department of Industrial Relations; Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board (OSHSB)
appliesTo: All outdoor places of employment in California (section 3395), with high-heat procedures for agriculture, construction, landscaping, oil and gas extraction and certain heavy transportation
Indoor work areas where the temperature equals or exceeds 82 degrees Fahrenheit when employees are present (section 3396), subject to listed exceptions
Supervisory and non-supervisory employees whose work should reasonably be anticipated to expose them to heat illness risk

sections.heading: Which California heat standards contain training requirements?

blocks.text: Two standards in the General Industry Safety Orders do: section 3395 for outdoor work and section 3396 for indoor work. Section 3395, cited as the Maria Isabel Vasquez Jimenez heat illness standard, "shall apply to all outdoor places of employment." Section 3396 applies "to all indoor work areas where the temperature equals or exceeds 82 degrees Fahrenheit when employees are present." Cal/OSHA's heat guidance notes that employers with both indoor and outdoor workplaces may be covered by both.

The Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board approved section 3396 on June 20, 2024, and it went into effect on July 23, 2024. Section 3395 dates from emergency rules in 2005; its last substantive amendment became operative on May 1, 2015, followed by a 2020 change without regulatory effect. Both standards sit alongside the general Injury and Illness Prevention Program rule; see [Cal/OSHA IIPP training requirements](/regulations/cal-osha-iipp-training-requirements). This page states the position as at November 2026.

sections.heading: Who must be trained, and when?

blocks.text: Each supervisory and non-supervisory employee must be trained before beginning work "that should reasonably be anticipated to result in exposure to the risk of heat illness." The trigger is the exposure, not the season. A new hire starting in an un-air-conditioned warehouse in February still needs training before work if heat exposure is reasonably anticipated in that role.

Scope matters for the indoor standard. Section 3396 does not apply to telework from a location of the employee's choice that the employer does not control, to emergency operations directly involved in protecting life or property, or to listed state prisons and local detention and juvenile facilities. It also excludes incidental exposures between 82 and 95 degrees Fahrenheit lasting less than 15 minutes in any 60-minute period, except in vehicles without effective air conditioning and in shipping or intermodal containers during loading and unloading.

Neither standard sets a fixed refresher interval. Employers commonly retrain before each hot season and whenever procedures change, but that is a practice choice; the legal trigger is training before exposure. See [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: What topics must employee heat illness training cover?

blocks.text: Both standards list nine topics, (A) to (I), in subsection (h)(1). The wording is nearly identical; the indoor version refers to cool-down areas and control measures where the outdoor version refers to shade.

blocks.text: Topics (G) to (I) depend on the site. An employee on a remote agricultural block and one in a city warehouse need different emergency instructions, so a single statewide module cannot cover them alone. Site-specific supplements or a supervisor briefing tied to the written plan fill that gap.

sections.heading: What extra training do supervisors need?

blocks.text: Supervisors must be trained before supervising heat-exposed work, on four topics in subsection (h)(2): everything in the employee training; the procedures they must follow to implement the standard; what to do when an employee shows signs or reports symptoms, including emergency response; and how to monitor weather reports and respond to hot weather advisories.

The indoor standard limits the weather topic to work areas "affected by outdoor temperatures." It also adds a note that where employees are covered by both standards, the section 3396 training "can be integrated into section 3395 training." For supervisors, the duties are operational: under section 3395(g), all employees must be closely observed during a heat wave, and newly assigned employees in a high heat area for their first 14 days. Section 3396(g) has parallel close observation duties for indoor work. Supervisors need to know how to run those observations, not only that they exist.

sections.heading: How do outdoor high-heat procedures affect training?

blocks.text: In listed industries, outdoor work at or above 95 degrees Fahrenheit adds pre-shift meetings that act as short refresher training. Section 3395(e) applies high-heat procedures to agriculture, construction, landscaping, oil and gas extraction, and transportation or delivery of agricultural products, construction materials or other heavy materials. The procedures include "Pre-shift meetings before the commencement of work to review the high heat procedures, encourage employees to drink plenty of water, and remind employees of their right to take a cool-down rest when necessary."

Shade must be present when the outdoor temperature exceeds 80 degrees Fahrenheit, and agricultural employees at 95 degrees or above must take a minimum ten minute net preventative cool-down rest every two hours. Training should teach employees these thresholds as they apply to their own crew, since they are the points at which the employer's duties change.

sections.heading: What does the indoor standard add on measurement and records?

blocks.text: Indoor work areas at 87 degrees Fahrenheit or more, or at 82 degrees with heat-restrictive clothing or high radiant heat, trigger assessment and control duties in section 3396(e). Employers must measure temperature and heat index, record whichever is greater with date, time and location, and keep the records for 12 months or until the next measurements, whichever is later. Employees and their union representatives must be actively involved in planning and recording measurements.

Neither heat standard sets a separate retention period for training records. Section 3203(b)(2) requires documentation of IIPP training for each employee for at least one year, and many employers record heat training in the same system so that the date of training can be compared with the date of first exposure. See [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: What must the written plan contain, and are the rules changing?

blocks.text: Both standards require an effective written Heat Illness Prevention Plan "in both English and the language understood by the majority of the employees," available at the worksite to employees and to Cal/OSHA on request. The outdoor plan covers water and shade, high-heat procedures, emergency response and acclimatization. The indoor plan adds procedures to measure temperature and heat index, evaluate other risk factors and implement control measures.

blocks.title: Status as at November 2026
blocks.text: The Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board's proposed regulations list, updated October 2026, contains no rulemaking notice for section 3395 or 3396. Both standards apply as published on the Department of Industrial Relations site.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each of the nine training topics to the matching section of the employer's written plan, so site-specific procedures such as EMS contact and directions to the worksite are taught from the current plan version. Exposure dates by role can then be compared with training dates. See [compliance programs](/programs/compliance).

faqs.q: Is Cal/OSHA heat illness training required every year?
faqs.a: Neither section 3395 nor section 3396 sets an annual interval. Both require training before an employee begins work reasonably expected to expose them to heat illness risk, and supervisor training before supervising that work. Many employers retrain each spring as good practice.

faqs.q: Do office workers need indoor heat training?
faqs.a: Only if their work area reaches 82 degrees Fahrenheit or more while they are present and no exception applies. Air-conditioned offices that stay below that threshold are outside section 3396, and telework from a location of the employee's choice is excluded.

faqs.q: Can outdoor and indoor heat training be combined?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 3396(h) states that where employees are covered by both standards, the indoor training program can be integrated into section 3395 training. The combined course should still cover indoor items such as cool-down areas and control measures.

faqs.q: What language must heat illness training be delivered in?
faqs.a: The standards require the written plan in English and in the language understood by the majority of employees. The training itself must be effective, which in practice means employees must understand it, so delivery in the languages your workforce uses is the safer approach.

factCheck.claim: Section 3395(a): Maria Isabel Vasquez Jimenez heat illness standard; applies to all outdoor places of employment; high-heat procedures apply to agriculture, construction, landscaping, oil and gas extraction, and transportation or delivery of agricultural products, construction materials or other heavy materials.

Section 3395(h)(1) nine topics (A) to (I) including up to 4 cups per hour; training before work reasonably anticipated to result in exposure; (h)(2) supervisor topics including weather reports; (i) plan in English and majority language; (d) shade above 80F; (e) 95F high-heat, pre-shift meetings, agricultural ten minute rest every two hours; (g) heat wave observation and 14 days for new employees; amendment operative 5-1-2015.

Section 3396(a): applies at 82F; (a)(2) 87F temperature or heat index, or 82F with restrictive clothing or high radiant heat; exceptions for telework, incidental exposure under 15 minutes in 60, emergency operations, prisons and local detention and juvenile facilities; new section operative 7-23-2024.

Section 3396(h): same nine topics with cool-down areas and control measures; supervisor weather topic only where work area affected by outdoor temperatures; note allowing integration with 3395 training; (e) measurement records kept 12 months or until next measurement, whichever is later.
OSHSB approved section 3396 on June 20, 2024; effective July 23, 2024; employers may be covered by both standards.
